tone_statements.citation: Sande, Hannah. 2022. Is grammatical tone item-based or process-based? Phonology 39(3): 399-442. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0952675723000106 (first published online 2 October 2023; CC BY 4.0).
tone_statements.quote: Guébie has four contrastive tone heights labelled 1–4, of which 4 is the highest. All morphemes, with the exception of the definite suffix (Sande 2017), are associated with an underlying tone melody, and surface with that tone melody unless some phonological or grammatical tonal alternation applies. Basic clausal word order is SAuxOV or SVO. There are many grammatical tone processes in the language. [...] Contrastive underlying tone melodies include levels 1, 2, 3 and 4 and contours 41, 42, 31, 32, 23 and 24. [...] Tone is the sole marker of imperfective aspect in Guébie.
tone_statements.locator: p. 409, sec. 2.2 'Guébie negation as adding a high tone' (first segment); p. 419, sec. 3.2 'Scalar tone shift in Guébie' (second and third segments)
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive level tone heights (1-4) plus lexical contours (41, 42, 31, 32, 23, 24) and a derived super-high 5; tone melodies are lexical on every morpheme and tone is heavily grammatical (negation adds H to the subject NP; imperfective is marked solely by a scalar tone shift); no statement about stress.

tone_statements.citation: Sande, Hannah, Peter Jenks & Sharon Inkelas. 2020. Cophonologies by Ph(r)ase. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 38(4): 1211-1261. Springer. doi:10.1007/s11049-020-09467-x (CC BY 4.0).
tone_statements.quote: In Guébie (Kru), the distinction between perfective and imperfective aspect is marked by a scalar shift in tone (Sande 2017, 2018). … Guébie has four underlying tone heights, 1–4 where 4 is high. In imperfective contexts, tone on a verbal head surfaces one step lower than in other contexts. … the lexically specified tone on the verb root [li], ‘eat’, is a level 3, a mid-high tone. … When the underlying verb tone is low (tone 1) (50a), it does not lower further to super-low (50c). Instead, the final tone of the subject raises one step (50b).
tone_statements.summary: Four level tone heights, numbered 1 (low) to 4 (high); imperfective aspect is marked by lowering the verb tone one step, or raising the subject's final tone when the verb is already low.

tone_statements.citation: Sande, Hannah. 2016. Scalar tone shift as evidence for morphology without morphemes. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 12(1): 103-125. doi:10.5070/P7121040724. eScholarship item 2993j1t2.
tone_statements.quote: Guébie is a tonal language with four distinct tone heights, marked here with numbers 1-4 where 4 is high [fn. 1]. Attested tone melodies on lexical roots include all level tones (1, 2, 3, 4), along with those contours represented in (1). [...] While all level tone melodies (heights 1-4) and seven of twelve possible two-tone contours given the four tone heights of Guébie are present on Guébie roots and affixes, none of these level or contour melodies triggers raising or lowering of nearby tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1 of the paper, sec. 2 'Guébie scalar tone shift'; second segment p. 5
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone language with four level tone heights (1-4) and two-tone contour melodies on roots and affixes; imperfective aspect realised by a scalar tone shift; nothing on stress.

sources.note: States the Guébie tone system and describes two grammatical tone processes in detail: four contrastive tone heights 1-4 (4 = high), a derived super-high 5 under grammatical raising, underlying level melodies 1-4 and contours 41, 42, 31, 32, 23, 24; every morpheme except the definite suffix carries an underlying tone melody; negation = an added H tone at the end of the subject NP's melody (table (7), p. 410); imperfective = scalar tone shift on the verb (lowering one step) or subject (raising), tone being the sole exponent of imperfective (sec. 3.2, pp. 419 ff.).

sources.citation: Sande, Hannah. 2021. Morpheme-specific phonology in reduplication. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 9 (AMP 2020). Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v9i0.4882 (CC BY 3.0).
sources.note: 'The first case study comes from Guébie (Kru, Ivory Coast), where reduplication marks both nominalization and reciprocals (among others). In both morphosyntactic environments, reduplication copies the verb plus valency-changing affixes, but the reduplicants are subject to different sets of phonotactic restrictions.' A Guébie phonology article not previously listed here; tone of the reduplicant is likely transcribed/discussed but tone is not its subject. Not downloaded (download budget spent on works 1-2).
